candidates.statement: In general, FDA’s guidance documents do not establish legally enforceable responsibilities. 26 Instead, guidances describe the Agency’s current thinking on a topic and should be viewed 27 only as recommendations, unless specific regulatory or statutory requirements are cited. The 28 use of the word should in Agency guidances means that something is suggested or 29 recommended, but not required. 30
candidates.context: This guidance provides recommendations for clinical trials designed to establish clinical 17 effectiveness and safety for hormonal drug products intended to prevent pregnancy 2 . Drug 18 product development in hormonal contraception has evolved over the years, especially with 19 the development of lower-dose hormonal drug products and longer-acting reversible 20 contraceptives. Changes in patient demographics, pregnancy testing, determinations of 21 conception date, and dosing directions have also occurred. This guidance reflects these 22 developments and is generally consistent with advice we have been providing to individual 23 sponsors developing hormonal drug products. 24 II. CLINICAL TRIAL DESIGN FEATURES—KEY CONSIDERATIONS 33

candidates.statement: The effectiveness of some contraceptives may be reduced with increasing body weight. Sponsors 57 should not place restrictions on body mass index (BMI) for trial enrollment. The trial population 58 should include obese women (i.e., defined as BMI of at least 30 kg/m 2 ), and the analysis plan 59 should include a prespecified subgroup efficacy analysis in this population. Insufficient data in 60 the obese population may result in a limitation of use for this population in labeling. During the 61 trial design phase, sponsors should discuss with the division the adequacy of the number of 62 cycles of drug exposure that will be derived from obese subjects. 63

candidates.statement: Randomizing subjects to placebo is not feasible because subjects in a contraceptive trial do not 75 desire pregnancy. Approximately 80% to 90% of women of reproductive potential who use no 76 contraception and engage in regular intercourse are expected to become pregnant within 1 year 77 (Guttmacher 1956; Zinaman et al. 1996; Wang et al. 2003; Gnoth et al. 2003; Slama et al. 2012), 78 and contraceptives typically have sizeable treatment effects. Therefore, single-arm, open-label, 79 historically controlled trials are generally sufficient to establish efficacy. Sponsors should discuss 80 with the division how they intend to ensure an accurate assessment of contraceptive 81 effectiveness, such as minimizing missing data and minimizing premature subject 82 discontinuation. 83

candidates.statement: Data from single-arm, open-label trials of at least 1 year’s duration are generally sufficient to 90 establish efficacy and safety, provided that the trials are well-conducted. Trials of longer 91 duration (covering the maximum duration of use proposed in labeling) are recommended for 92 long-acting reversible contraceptives, such as intrauterine systems. Trials of shorter duration may 93 be sufficient for products containing drug substances that already have well-characterized safety 94 profiles. Sponsors should discuss the adequacy of the trial duration with the division. 95

candidates.statement: Urine pregnancy tests should be performed regularly at clinic visits, including at the end of the 107 study or with premature subject discontinuation. Sponsors should provide subjects with home 108 pregnancy test kits for use in case of signs and symptoms of pregnancy or multiple missed 109 contraceptive doses. candidates.statement: On-treatment pregnancy should be defined as any pregnancy that occurs during use of the 127 product or within a specific timeframe after last use of the product. Some examples are provided 128 below. Sponsors should discuss with the division the appropriate timeframe after last use for 129 other scenarios. 130
candidates.context: C. Efficacy Considerations 125 For contraceptives that require daily administration (e.g., oral combined hormonal 132 contraceptives), last use includes the use of the product from the placebo (or drug-free days) or 133 estrogen-only phase of the regimen. A positive pregnancy test within 7 days of this last use 134 would be considered on-treatment (a detected pregnancy in this timeframe reflects conception 135 that occurred when pregnancy should still have been prevented). For example, if a woman’s 136 estimated date of conception is 7 days after she completed Day 28 of a 21/7 (active/placebo) 137 regimen, a positive pregnancy test would be considered on-treatment. 138

candidates.context: Calculation of the PI for the primary efficacy evaluation should include only cycles during which 156 (a) vaginal intercourse occurred and (b) no backup or emergency contraception was used based 157 on diary data. 158 The assessment of efficacy is based on the point estimate and the upper bound of the 164 corresponding 95% confidence interval for the PI. Combined hormonal contraceptives are very 165 effective at preventing pregnancy, typically having an upper bound of this 95% confidence 166 interval below 5 in adequately designed and conducted trials. For hormonal contraceptives with 167 fewer risks, such as oral progestin-only contraceptives, a slightly higher upper bound of this 95% 168 confidence interval may be acceptable. 169

candidates.statement: The primary efficacy results should be calculated using the trial population of women younger 171 than or equal to 35 years old at study enrollment because the likelihood of pregnancy decreases 172 with advancing age. Include additional efficacy analyses for the overall trial population and a 173 subgroup analysis for those older than 35 years old. 174

candidates.context: D. Safety Considerations 188 Hormonal contraceptives have well-known risks, some of which are infrequent, such as venous 193 thromboembolism. The division may require postmarketing evaluation of risks such as venous 194 thromboembolism if the benefits of a new drug product outweigh its risks, but additional 195 characterization of the risk is required postapproval. 196
